front: Adult primary care visit: who gets depression screening, is suicide screening recommended, and what is first-line treatment?

bullets.clue: PHQ-2, then PHQ-9; ask directly about suicide if positive.
bullets.treat: Psychotherapy or antidepressant by preference; psychotherapy first if pregnant.
bullets.trap: Universal suicide screening is an I statement.

back: Screen all adults for depression. Key clue: PHQ-2, then PHQ-9; ask directly about suicide if positive. First-line: Psychotherapy or antidepressant by preference; psychotherapy first if pregnant. Exam trap: Universal suicide screening is an I statement.

diagram.alt: All adults are screened for depression with PHQ-2 then PHQ-9, treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant by preference; universal suicide screening has insufficient evidence but depressed patients are asked directly.

source.guideline: USPSTF Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); VA/DoD MDD Guideline (2022)
source.recommendation: USPSTF 2023: screen all adults incl. pregnant/postpartum and older adults for depression (B); suicide-risk screening I. VA/DoD 2022: psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy monotherapy by preference; psychotherapy first-line for mild-moderate MDD in pregnancy/breastfeeding and suggested for older adults.

front: Mania with decreased need for sleep: first-line drugs for mania, bipolar depression and maintenance?
bottom: Lithium or quetiapine; avoid antidepressant monotherapy.

bullets.clue: ≥1 week elevated mood, less sleep, grandiosity.
bullets.treat: Mania: lithium or quetiapine. Bipolar depression: quetiapine. Maintenance: lithium or quetiapine.

back: Lithium or quetiapine; avoid antidepressant monotherapy. Key clue: ≥1 week elevated mood, less sleep, grandiosity. First-line: Mania: lithium or quetiapine. Bipolar depression: quetiapine. Maintenance: lithium or quetiapine. Exam trap: Antidepressants alone can trigger mania.

diagram.alt: Bipolar disorder: lithium or quetiapine for mania and maintenance, quetiapine for bipolar depression, no antidepressant monotherapy, and lithium toxicity near 1.5 mEq/L.

source.guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Bipolar Disorder (2023); FDA lithium label
source.recommendation: VA/DoD 2023: suggest lithium or quetiapine for acute mania; recommend quetiapine for acute bipolar depression; lamotrigine with lithium or quetiapine suggested; recommend lithium or quetiapine to prevent mania recurrence; insufficient evidence for antidepressant monotherapy; algorithm says continue to avoid antidepressants. FDA label: toxic ≥1.5 mEq/L.

front: Excessive worry most days for 6 months vs sudden attacks of chest tightness and fear: diagnosis and first-line care?
bottom: GAD or panic disorder: CBT or SSRI/SNRI.

bullets.clue: GAD: 6 months of worry. Panic: recurrent attacks, fear of more.
bullets.treat: CBT, SSRI or SNRI; screen adults 64 and younger.

back: GAD or panic disorder: CBT or SSRI/SNRI. Key clue: GAD: 6 months of worry. Panic: recurrent attacks, fear of more. First-line: CBT, SSRI or SNRI; screen adults 64 and younger. Exam trap: Avoid long-term benzodiazepines.

diagram.alt: Generalized anxiety and panic disorder screened in adults 64 and younger and treated with CBT or an SSRI or SNRI, after ruling out thyroid, cardiac and substance causes; avoid long-term benzodiazepines.

source.guideline: USPSTF Anxiety Disorders in Adults: Screening (2023)
source.recommendation: USPSTF 2023: screen adults ≤64 incl. pregnant/postpartum for anxiety (B); ≥65 I statement. Treatment can include psychotherapy (e.g., CBT) and pharmacotherapy.

front: Schizophrenia on an antipsychotic: when to use clozapine, and how to treat dystonia, akathisia and tardive dyskinesia?
bottom: Clozapine for resistance or suicide risk; VMAT2 inhibitor for TD.

bullets.treat: Acute dystonia: anticholinergic. Akathisia: lower dose, propranolol. TD: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine.

back: Clozapine for resistance or suicide risk; VMAT2 inhibitor for TD. Key clue: Psychosis ≥6 months; failed two antipsychotics. First-line: Acute dystonia: anticholinergic. Akathisia: lower dose, propranolol. TD: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine. Exam trap: Clozapine needs ANC monitoring.

diagram.alt: Schizophrenia: clozapine for treatment resistance or ongoing suicide risk; anticholinergic for acute dystonia, dose reduction or beta-blocker for akathisia, VMAT2 inhibitor for tardive dyskinesia, plus metabolic monitoring.

source.guideline: APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia (2020)
source.recommendation: APA 2020: clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (1B) and substantial suicide risk (1B); anticholinergic for acute dystonia (1C); akathisia: lower dose, switch, benzodiazepine or beta-blocker (2C); VMAT2 inhibitor for moderate-severe TD (1B). Metabolic: weight each visit for 6 months; glucose/lipids at 4 months then annually.

front: Opioid use disorder: which medications, how to start buprenorphine, and who gets naloxone?
bottom: Offer buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone; naloxone for all.

bullets.clue: Craving, tolerance, withdrawal, use despite harm.
bullets.treat: Buprenorphine once withdrawal starts; methadone in programs; naltrexone after detox.

back: Offer buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone; naloxone for all. Key clue: Craving, tolerance, withdrawal, use despite harm. First-line: Buprenorphine once withdrawal starts; methadone in programs; naltrexone after detox. Exam trap: No X-waiver needed since 2023.

diagram.alt: Opioid use disorder treated with buprenorphine started once withdrawal begins, methadone through a treatment program, or naltrexone after detox, with naloxone for every patient; no X-waiver is needed since 2023.

source.guideline: ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update; SAMHSA MAT Act waiver elimination (2023)
source.recommendation: ASAM 2020: methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone recommended; buprenorphine after objective withdrawal; extended-release naltrexone for patients no longer physically dependent; declining psychosocial treatment should not delay medication; naloxone for patients and families. SAMHSA: 2023 Act removed the X-waiver.

front: A 5-year-old vs an 8-year-old with ADHD: first-line treatment for each?
bottom: Age 4–5: behavior therapy first. Age 6+: medication plus behavior therapy.

bullets.treat: Parent training first; stimulant if age 6+ or still impaired.

back: Age 4–5: behavior therapy first. Age 6+: medication plus behavior therapy. Key clue: Symptoms in ≥2 settings before age 12. First-line: Parent training first; stimulant if age 6+ or still impaired. Exam trap: Check cardiac history before stimulants.

diagram.alt: ADHD in children 4 to 5 treated first with parent training and classroom behavior interventions, methylphenidate only if still impaired; ages 6 to 11 get FDA-approved medication plus behavioral therapy and school supports.

source.guideline: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD in Children and Adolescents (2019)
source.recommendation: AAP 2019: ages 4–5: PTBM and/or behavioral classroom interventions first (A); methylphenidate if moderate-severe disturbance persists (B). Ages 6–11: FDA-approved ADHD medication plus PTBM and/or classroom interventions, preferably both (A); educational supports (IEP/504).

front: Nightmares and flashbacks after combat vs intrusive thoughts with hand-washing rituals: first-line treatment?
bottom: PTSD: trauma-focused therapy. OCD: ERP or SSRI.

bullets.clue: PTSD: re-experiencing >1 month after trauma. OCD: obsessions plus compulsions.
bullets.treat: PTSD: CPT, PE or EMDR; or sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine. OCD: ERP or SSRI.
bullets.trap: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD.

back: PTSD: trauma-focused therapy. OCD: ERP or SSRI. Key clue: PTSD: re-experiencing >1 month after trauma. OCD: obsessions plus compulsions. First-line: PTSD: CPT, PE or EMDR; or sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine. OCD: ERP or SSRI. Exam trap: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD.

diagram.alt: PTSD treated with trauma-focused psychotherapy such as CPT, prolonged exposure or EMDR, or sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine, never benzodiazepines; OCD treated with exposure and response prevention or an SSRI.

source.guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for PTSD and Acute Stress Disorder (2023); APA Practice Guideline for OCD
source.recommendation: VA/DoD 2023: recommend CPT, EMDR or PE; recommend paroxetine, sertraline or venlafaxine; recommend against benzodiazepines and cannabis. APA OCD: CBT with ERP and SRIs first-line; combine after inadequate monotherapy or if severe.

front: Underweight teen with bradycardia vs normal-weight binge-purge cycles: first steps?
bottom: Anorexia: medical stability, then nutrition. Bulimia: CBT plus fluoxetine.

bullets.clue: Anorexia: low weight, restriction. Bulimia: binge-purge, normal weight.
bullets.treat: Anorexia: family-based treatment, monitored refeeding. Bulimia: CBT and fluoxetine 60 mg.

back: Anorexia: medical stability, then nutrition. Bulimia: CBT plus fluoxetine. Key clue: Anorexia: low weight, restriction. Bulimia: binge-purge, normal weight. First-line: Anorexia: family-based treatment, monitored refeeding. Bulimia: CBT and fluoxetine 60 mg. Exam trap: Refeeding drops phosphate; monitor electrolytes.

diagram.alt: Anorexia nervosa managed with medical stabilization, weight goals and monitored refeeding with phosphate checks; bulimia nervosa treated with CBT plus fluoxetine 60 mg daily.

source.guideline: APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Eating Disorders (2023)
source.recommendation: APA 2023: individualized weight goals in anorexia; monitor electrolytes incl. phosphorus for refeeding risk; family-based treatment for adolescents with anorexia; adults with bulimia: eating-disorder CBT plus an SSRI (e.g., fluoxetine 60 mg).

front: Unstable relationships and self-harm vs a patient who blames others for his own feelings: personality disorder and defense?
bottom: Borderline: structured psychotherapy. Name the defense mechanism.

bullets.clue: Splitting: all good or all bad. Projection: own feelings onto others.
bullets.treat: Borderline: DBT or similar psychotherapy; medication only for target symptoms.
bullets.trap: No drug treats borderline personality disorder itself.

back: Borderline: structured psychotherapy. Name the defense mechanism. Key clue: Splitting: all good or all bad. Projection: own feelings onto others. First-line: Borderline: DBT or similar psychotherapy; medication only for target symptoms. Exam trap: No drug treats borderline personality disorder itself.

diagram.alt: Personality disorder clusters A odd, B dramatic, C anxious; borderline personality disorder treated with structured psychotherapy such as DBT, medication only as a short adjunct; splitting and projection defense mechanisms.

source.guideline: APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Borderline Personality Disorder (2024)
source.recommendation: APA 2024: structured evidence-based psychotherapy targeting BPD (e.g., DBT, mentalization-based treatment); medication adjunctive, time-limited, for specific symptoms or comorbidity, reviewed periodically.

front: Agitation, fever and a neuromuscular exam: which finding separates serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
bottom: Serotonin: clonus and hyperreflexia within 24 hours. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity over days.

bullets.treat: Stop the drug; cool, benzodiazepines. Serotonin: cyproheptadine. NMS: dantrolene or bromocriptine.

back: Serotonin: clonus and hyperreflexia within 24 hours. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity over days. Key clue: Both cause fever. First-line: Stop the drug; cool, benzodiazepines. Serotonin: cyproheptadine. NMS: dantrolene or bromocriptine. Exam trap: Bromocriptine worsens serotonin syndrome.

diagram.alt: Serotonin syndrome with clonus and hyperreflexia within a day, treated by stopping serotonergic drugs and cyproheptadine; neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity over days, treated with dantrolene or bromocriptine.

source.guideline: Hunter criteria and NMS/serotonin syndrome reviews; FDA lithium label
source.recommendation: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter): spontaneous clonus, or inducible/ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; stop serotonergic drugs; cyproheptadine for moderate-severe. NMS: rigidity, slower onset; dantrolene and/or bromocriptine; bromocriptine can worsen serotonin syndrome. Lithium: no specific antidote (label).

front: Infant with a bruise and a parent's story that doesn't fit vs an older adult with unexplained injuries: next steps?
bottom: Reasonable suspicion: report; certainty is not required.

bullets.clue: Sentinel injury in a baby who cannot cruise.
bullets.treat: Under 2: skeletal survey; report to CPS. Elders: adult protective services.
bullets.trap: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is abuse until proven otherwise.

back: Reasonable suspicion: report; certainty is not required. Key clue: Sentinel injury in a baby who cannot cruise. First-line: Under 2: skeletal survey; report to CPS. Elders: adult protective services. Exam trap: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is abuse until proven otherwise.

diagram.alt: Suspected child abuse in children under 2 gets a full exam and skeletal survey and a report on reasonable suspicion; women of reproductive age are screened for partner violence; suspected elder abuse is reported to adult protective services.

source.guideline: AAP Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse (2015); USPSTF Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse Screening (2025)
source.recommendation: AAP: children <2 with injuries concerning for abuse: complete skeletal survey; consider neuroimaging (<1 y); report on reasonable suspicion. USPSTF: screen reproductive-age women for IPV (B); insufficient evidence for screening older or vulnerable adults for abuse (I).

front: Altered patient in the ED: which pupil and vital-sign findings separate stimulant from opioid intoxication?
bottom: Dilated pupils, tachycardia: stimulant. Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing: opioid.

bullets.treat: Stimulant: benzodiazepines, aspirin for chest pain. Opioid: naloxone.
bullets.trap: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can seize; taper slowly.

back: Dilated pupils, tachycardia: stimulant. Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing: opioid. Key clue: Stimulant use disorder: contingency management. First-line: Stimulant: benzodiazepines, aspirin for chest pain. Opioid: naloxone. Exam trap: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can seize; taper slowly.

diagram.alt: Stimulant intoxication with dilated pupils treated with benzodiazepines and contingency management for use disorder; opioid toxidrome with pinpoint pupils; cannabinoid hyperemesis cured by stopping cannabis; benzodiazepines tapered 5 to 10 percent every 2 to 4 weeks.

source.guideline: ASAM/AAAP Stimulant Use Disorder Guideline (2023); AGA Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Update (2024); Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering (2025)
source.recommendation: ASAM/AAAP: contingency management is the best-supported psychosocial treatment for stimulant use disorder. AGA 2024: cannabis cessation is definitive for CHS. Benzodiazepine tapering guideline 2025: gradual supervised taper, generally 5–10% every 2–4 weeks; avoid abrupt discontinuation; typically not faster than 25% every 2 weeks.

front: Toddler with no pointing or words at 18 months: which screen, when, and what next?
bottom: Autism: screen at 18 and 24 months with M-CHAT-R/F.

bullets.clue: Poor eye contact, no pointing, repetitive behaviors.
bullets.treat: Positive screen: refer for diagnosis, early intervention and hearing test.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for diagnosis to start early intervention.

back: Autism: screen at 18 and 24 months with M-CHAT-R/F. Key clue: Poor eye contact, no pointing, repetitive behaviors. First-line: Positive screen: refer for diagnosis, early intervention and hearing test. Exam trap: Do not wait for diagnosis to start early intervention.

diagram.alt: Developmental screening at 9, 18 and 30 months and autism screening with M-CHAT-R/F at 18 and 24 months; positive screens are referred for diagnosis, hearing testing and early intervention.

source.guideline: AAP Developmental Surveillance and Screening; AAP Autism Identification and Evaluation
source.recommendation: AAP: developmental surveillance at every well visit; general developmental screening at 9, 18 and 30 months; ASD-specific screening at 18 and 24 months (M-CHAT-R/F commonly used).
